newsitem.title: USA: Kodak has lower quarter, higher year.
newsitem.headline: Kodak has lower quarter, higher year.

text.p: Eastman Kodak Co. Thursday reported lower fourth-quarter profits but higher earnings for the year as it continued efforts to cut costs.
Investors applauded the results, boosting Kodak's stock $4.25 to $85.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The world's largest maker of photographic film said it earned $164 million, or 49 cents per share, in the quarter, compared with profits of $275 million, or 80 cents a share, in the 1995 quarter.

Excluding restructuring costs, the loss on the sale of its office imaging operations and earnings from discontinued operations, fourth-quarter earnings were $395 million, or $1.19 a share, Kodak said.
Sales grew 5.4 percent to $4.31 billion from $4.09 billion.

For the year, Kodak earned $1.29 billion, or $3.82 a share, compared with $1.25 billion, or $3.67 a share a year earlier. Excluding restructuring and other costs, its profits in 1996 were $1.52 billion, or $4.50 per share.
Sales rose 6.6 percent to $15.97 billion from $14.98 billion.

Chief Financial Officer Harry Kavetas said Kodak invested $200 million in film manufacturing operations last May, and planned to boost spending on research and development, advertising and sales promotion.
"I'm confident we'll increase our expenditures in both areas," he said, although declined to be more specific.
The company spent $1.25 billion on advertising and sales promotions and $1.28 billion on research and development in 1996, he said.
Eastman Kodak Chairman George Fisher said in a statement that the company continues to improve its costs.
The company said it has seen growth in emerging markets, including China, Russia and Eastern Europe, although it did not provide specific figures.

A Kodak spokesman said the company's restructuring shows how it is seeking to improve its cost structure. The restructuring is the result of Kodak's efforts to eliminate redundancies and streamline worldwide operations, he said.
Kodak took a charge of $256 million for after-tax restructuring costs in the fourth quarter. It also recorded an after-tax loss of $252 million for the sale of its Office Imaging business.
Prudential Securities analyst Alexander Henderson said Kodak's restructuring moves, as well as its intention to refrain from increasing its workforce this year, should improve earnings, he added.

Prudential raised its 1997 earnings estimate for Kodak to $5.15 a share from $5, and its 1998 estimate to $5.95 per share from $5.80. Prudential also raised its 12-month price target to $100 per share from $95.
